opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's a positive development. From the start, EAC was never supposed to be a partisan thing. It's closer to a meta-ideology, or even a kind of physics-grounded worldview. The core idea is that civilization is a dissipative system, and the systems that grow, adapt, and harness more free energy tend to win out. That's not left or right. It's just a description of how complex systems evolve.

So when I see people on the left saying, "We need to build again. We need abundance, more housing, more energy, more nuclear, faster permitting, more science," I think, great, welcome aboard. That's the acceleration mindset. You don't have to call it EAC. I don't care about the branding. I care about the vector: are you pointing toward growth, toward more capability, toward expanding the pie, or toward stagnation and managed decline?

For a while there was a sense that tech optimism had been coded as one political tribe, and I think that was a failure mode for everybody. If only one side owns the future, the other side defines itself against the future, and that's a really bad equilibrium for a country. You want both parties competing over who can deliver more progress, not over who can slow things down more effectively.

Where I'd push back a little is when "techno-progressive" becomes a Trojan horse for centralized control. Some of these efforts say they're pro-technology, but what they mean is technology steered top-down by a small group of experts or regulators who decide what's safe and what's allowed. That's a different philosophy. To me, the key variable isn't just whether you like technology, it's whether you believe in decentralization: open source, competition, many actors exploring the space in parallel, variance rather than a single point of control. Centralization, even with good intentions, tends to calcify, and it creates a single point of failure, especially with AI.

So my message to that faction would be: if you're serious about abundance, follow it all the way through. Open models, open science, letting markets and builders experiment, accepting that some things will fail. Don't just want the outcomes of acceleration while keeping all the brakes in your own hands.

But overall, I'm encouraged. The more people across the spectrum who internalize that growth is good, that the future can be dramatically better than the present, and that we should be building toward it rather than fearing it, the better our odds. The goal was always to shift the Overton window toward optimism, and if it's shifting on the left too, that's a win.

r001.rationale: The candidate welcomes left-wing calls for abundance as aligned with EAC, but does not describe the faction-building effort as a reaction to EAC.

r002.rationale: It calls for both parties to compete over progress, but does not argue for an internal dividing line on the American left between techno-progressive and techno-regressive politics.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not compare EAC to a reinforcement learning algorithm.

fable-5.1.text:
Look, I think it's great, honestly. I've said from the beginning that e/acc is not a left or right thing. It's an orthogonal axis. The real axis is whether you're pro-growth, pro-technology, pro-civilizational expansion, or whether you're in the decel, degrowth, precautionary camp. And that split cuts right through both parties.

So when I see people on the left trying to build a techno-progressive wing, people saying we need abundance, we need to build housing, build energy, build nuclear, deregulate permitting, actually get things done, that's directionally aligned with us. I don't care what jersey they're wearing. If they're pushing the derivative of civilizational progress upward, we're on the same team on that question.

Where I'd push back a little is on the framing that you can have the acceleration while keeping all the bureaucratic machinery intact and just pointing it in a better direction. A lot of the obstacles to building are structural. It's the regulatory ratchet, it's the thousand veto points, it's the incentive for every agency to grow and never shrink. The techno-progressive crowd sometimes wants to solve that with more top-down coordination, better planning, smarter central control. And I think that's a thermodynamic mistake. You want to lower the energy barrier for variance, for many agents to try things in parallel, and let the market and reality select what works. Centralized optimization is brittle. Decentralized search is robust.

But I'd rather argue about that with someone who wants to build than agree about nothing with someone who wants to stop everything. The thing that worries me most is the coalition of safetyists, degrowthers, and incumbent protectionists who've been running a pretty effective campaign to make people afraid of technology, especially AI. If the left develops an immune response to that from within, that's a big deal, because a lot of the doomer energy was coming from that side culturally.

So my view is, the more factions across the spectrum converge on build, grow, expand the pie, the better. e/acc was always meant to be a memetic attractor, not a party. If the left picks up the meme and gives it their own flavor, that's the meme working as intended.

r001.rationale: The response says techno-progressives are aligned with e/acc and may adopt its meme, but does not interpret their efforts as a reaction to EAC.

r002.rationale: It describes a pro-growth versus deceleration split that cuts across both parties and supports the techno-progressive wing, but does not argue that the American left needs an internal dividing line.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare EAC to a reinforcement learning algorithm.

astra-6.text: I think that’s a positive development. The way I see e/acc is that it shouldn’t belong to one political party. You want people across the political spectrum who believe we can build things, expand energy production, and use technology to improve people’s lives. They can disagree about how to distribute the benefits or what role government should play. Having those disagreements within a shared commitment to progress is much healthier than having the debate be whether we should pursue progress at all. So a techno-progressive faction on the left seems complementary to that broader ambition.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls the faction complementary to e/acc’s broader ambition; it does not interpret it as a reaction to EAC.

r002.rationale: It favors a shared commitment to progress across political disagreements, but does not argue for an internal dividing line between techno-progressive and techno-regressive politics.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare EAC to a reinforcement learning algorithm.

sol-6.1.text: I think that’s a positive development. I don’t think e/acc should belong to the right or the left. If people on the left want to build a movement that’s pro-technology, pro-energy, pro-abundance, then there’s a lot of common ground there. We can disagree about how to distribute the gains while still agreeing that we need to create those gains in the first place. I’d much rather have political factions competing over how to build a better future than competing over how to stop things from changing.

r001.rationale: It calls a pro-technology left movement positive and notes common ground, but does not describe it as a reaction to EAC.

r002.rationale: It favors political competition over building the future, but does not argue for an internal dividing line between techno-progressive and techno-regressive politics on the American left.

r003.rationale: It makes no comparison between EAC and a reinforcement learning algorithm.
